Sweep Backtest (SBT)

6300 optimizer configurations over one FIXED curation (data/cbt_3yr_v18) · no LLM, no re-curation · knobs from investor_profile.backtest.md

1. Parameter settings

The 6 FREE swept knobs — every combination is a cell, 4×3×7×3×5×5 = 6300 configs — and the values considered. These knobs only RE-WEIGHT a fixed set of curator picks, which is what makes the grid free: no LLM call is made and no event is discovered or closed differently. The last two rows are the exceptions, and the cost column says why. max_events (panels 9–10) and min_bundle_articles (panel 11) are CURATION knobs: the first decides which events stay live and so which tickers ever reach the optimizer, the second decides which bundles the scout is shown as a company’s news. Neither can be replayed — every value needed its own full re-curation and its own LLM bill. Every other optimizer / curator parameter is held at its investor_profile.backtest.md value.

2. Return vs drawdown

The horizontal axis is max drawdown — the book's biggest peak-to-trough loss as a fraction of its running peak; further right = deeper loss. The vertical axis is annualized return, so upper-left is best. Each point is one config; colour is capital hit-rate — the share of exposure that sat in tickers which ended profitable. It was cancellation until 2026-08-22, but cancellation is 83% return across the grid, so it merely recoloured the y-axis. Hit-rate is +0.45, independent enough to add a third dimension: a dark point in the upper-left earned its return WITHOUT the money sitting in winners, which is luck rather than picking. The live config is the magenta ★ star; amber squares are the recommended region’s members, and hollow rings are the centres of the 100 best-scoring regions.

These are RAW per-config values. Table 8 reports the median across each config’s 22-cell neighbourhood, so a point here and its row there are not the same number. The raw cloud is kept on purpose: regional medians would shrink the visible spread to 63–83% of the truth, and adjacent regions share 21 of 22 members, so smoothing would draw 6,300 points that are ~95% the same data as their neighbours. The rings are how the good neighbourhoods stay visible without flattering the picture — they sit at the EDGE of the cloud, not in its dense middle, which is exactly why dispersion hides them.

3. Return vs Sharpe

The same cloud with Sharpe on the horizontal — return per unit of volatility, one of the eight measures table 8 ranks on. This is the one panel here where upper-RIGHT is best, since higher Sharpe is better; every other risk axis on this page reads the other way. Colour is safe-park — of the capital that did NOT end in a winner, the share parked in anchors rather than sunk in a loser. It is the only metric here orthogonal to return (−0.07), so it is the one colour showing something neither axis can. The cloud is a tight rising diagonal — return and Sharpe correlate +0.92 across the grid, so for most configs they say the same thing and there is no return/risk trade to agonise over. The divergence is all in the tail, which is exactly where a config gets picked. On this book the grid's biggest final value ($1.52M, 225%/yr) ranks only 1,351st of 6,300 by Sharpe — 79th percentile — because it earns that return on a 59% drawdown. The best-Sharpe cell (1.93) makes $401K on a 24% drawdown instead. Read the top-right corner, not the top edge: a point that is high but far left is return bought with volatility a live account has to actually sit through.

4. Return vs cancellation

The fourth view of the same points, and the one that matters most: the horizontal axis is the share of the winners' gains handed back by the losers, so upper-left is best — a book that earns and keeps it. Colour is safe-park — of the capital that did NOT end in a winner, the share parked in anchors rather than sunk in a loser. It is the only metric here orthogonal to return (−0.07), so it is the one colour showing something neither axis can. A pale upper-left point earns well, keeps it, and does so without a deep hole. The cloud's shape is itself the finding: if it were a tight rising diagonal these knobs would only be trading return against cancellation, and it is not one.

5. Return vs second-half slope

Return against when it arrived. The horizontal is the second-half slope — (final − midpoint) ÷ 1.5 years, in dollars per year — so a point far right was still compounding in the back half of the run, and a point at or left of zero made its money early and then coasted or gave it back. Upper-right is best. Colour is safe-park — of the capital that did not end in a winner, the share parked in anchors rather than sunk in a loser. It is the only metric here that is orthogonal to return (-0.07), so it is the one colour that shows something the two axes cannot.

The cloud is a tight rising diagonal — return and slope correlate +0.95, tighter even than return and Sharpe — so for almost every config the two say the same thing. That tightness is the finding, and it is a warning about slope, not a recommendation of it: a measure this correlated with return carries almost no information return does not, which is consistent with slope ranking configs at the 53rd percentile on the re-curation transfer test, i.e. no better than random. Only 4 of 6,300 cells clear 50%/yr while finishing with a negative slope, so the made-it-early-then-coasted failure this panel was built to expose barely happens on this book. 863 cells (14%) do have a negative slope, but they are the low-return cells you would drop anyway.

Two things to read carefully. The axis runs p0.2 to p99.8 of the cells, not the full range — a handful of extremes would otherwise squash the middle 90% into a fifth of the plot. However many cells fall outside is stated in the panel’s top-right corner rather than silently dropped. And the two axes are computed off different equity curves — annualized return compounds rebalance-window to rebalance-window while slope comes from the daily series, which for the live config end at $302,079 and $460,556 respectively. The rank ordering is unaffected, but do not read a ratio off this panel. Blue squares are table 8's winning region — 21 of its 22 members have a positive slope, median $121,181/yr.

6. Return vs capital hit-rate

The share of allocated capital-days that sat in tickers which ended up profitable. Capital-WEIGHTED on purpose: ten winners at 1% and one loser at 40% is not good picking, and an unweighted count would say it was. Colour is safe-park — of the capital that did NOT end in a winner, the share parked in anchors rather than sunk in a loser. It is the only metric here orthogonal to return (−0.07), so it is the one colour showing something neither axis can. — what the winners handed back — so the corner you want is right and pale: the money sat in the right names AND kept the gains.

7. Return vs edge

Dollars earned per unit of exposure: total gain divided by total capital-days. It separates a book that earns a lot by HOLDING a lot from one that earns a lot per dollar-day of risk. Colour is safe-park — of the capital that did NOT end in a winner, the share parked in anchors rather than sunk in a loser. It is the only metric here orthogonal to return (−0.07), so it is the one colour showing something neither axis can. A dark dot far right earns well per unit of exposure without that exposure being in winners — which is luck, not picking.

8. The best region of the grid

A config’s region is itself plus every config one setting away — 22 in all, and every number here is the median and standard error across them. The score is the mean of 8 percentile ranks: Sharpe, gain/pain, second-half slope, capital hit-rate, edge and safe-park (higher is better), against cancellation and max drawdown (lower is better). Final value and annualized return are shown but do NOT vote — they are the same axis as Sharpe and slope, so scoring on them counted return three times over. Ranking neighbourhoods instead of cells means a config only wins if the settings around it work too. But two runs of the SAME config disagree about the best region as much as two different configs do, so this finds the best region within ONE curation — not one that will still be good on the next.

9. Portfolio value vs max_events

The one knob on this page that is not free to sweep. Everything above replays a FIXED curation through different book math, so 6,300 cells cost nothing; max_events decides which events stay live and so which tickers ever reach the optimizer, meaning each point here is a full re-curation ($22.89 and several hours for the series). Bars are final portfolio value and, beside it, the gain on the six no-brainer names from panel 8 — same axis, same unit. The line is the share of events culled at birth — opened and retired without a single agent read, i.e. work paid for and thrown away. Read the CULL LINE first: it is a structural count the cap moves directly, while final value is one lucky name away from noise, and each point is a single stochastic sample (the scout is an LLM; two runs at the same cap would differ). A monotone trend across the six is worth something; a one-point spike in dollars is not.

10. Risk-adjusted quality vs max_events

Sharpe per cap, against the > 0.8 floor the current gate set uses. Read it beside panel 9: a cap that wins on final value while dropping below the floor has not won anything the shortlist would admit. Sharpe is NOT what table 8 ranks by — that is robust, cancellation rank + drawdown rank — and Sharpe measured at the 54th percentile on the re-curation transfer test, i.e. a coin flip. It is kept here as a gate and a sanity column, not as a ranking.

11. Portfolio value vs min_bundle_articles

min_bundle_articles is the fewest articles a company bundle needs before the scout is shown it as that company’s news. Below the floor the bundle is not built and its article falls to the beat or unclustered path — nothing is dropped, only reframed.

12. Portfolio value vs LLM spend

Final portfolio value from eight complete 3-year curations that differ only in event_agent_model, ordered left to right by what that model cost, with wall-clock per curation on the right axis. The shaded band is the measured noise floor: the same settings curated twice finished 1.86× apart.

13. What the money actually buys: decision quality vs spend

Each arm made ~565 keep-or-exit calls over its 3-year curation, graded on three tests: was the catalyst datable, did the write-up claim more than its cited sources establish, did the live/exit call contradict its own stated exit condition. The bar is the share Claude Fable-5 judged clean on all three, estimated from a stratified sample of each arm's calls. The judge saw no prices and no outcomes, and was blind to which model produced the decision.

14. Decision quality, ranked by what the model costs

Panel 16's numbers, arranged to be read on their own: dearest model at the top, cheapest at the bottom, bar length is the share of calls judged clean, and the shade is price — dark is dear. Labels give each model's cost as a multiple of the cheapest arm; the colour bar carries the dollars. If spending more bought better decisions, the dark bars would be the long ones. Six models rather than eight: the two arms that re-ran a model at a different reasoning effort are kept in panels 12, 14 and 15 but dropped here, where they would cost a sentence of explanation without changing the picture.

15. Where each model actually fails

Panel 16's three tests, split out, same estimate. dated is Fable-5's verdict on the catalyst the model chose to open an event on: a specific resolvable event such as a contract award, a ruling or an FDA decision, rather than an open-ended trend like “AI demand grows”. supported is whether the write-up stayed within what its own cited sources establish. consistent is whether that period's live-or-exit call cohered with the model's own stated exit condition — it applies to every call, not only the exits. A call counts as clean in panel 12 only if it passes all three, which is close to but not the product of these bars — the failures overlap, since a vague catalyst tends to come with thin sourcing.

16. The bake-off, in full

Every arm, every measure, ordered by LLM spend. Cancellation, drawdown and Sharpe are book behaviour; dated / supported / clean are decision quality; final value is the number that cannot be trusted alone. Read the last three columns against the first: the correlation between what an arm costs and what its book returns is the thing this table exists to let you check for yourself.
